summary: This informational document sets out a framework for traceability in the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS). It explains the motivation, requirements and use cases, and defines an information model for recording interactions between I2RS components. The goal is a consistent way to log what was done, by which component, and when, which helps with operating and debugging the system.

plainLanguage.summary: When software changes a router's routes, it is useful to have a record of who asked for the change, what was asked for, what was actually done and what came back. This document defines the fields such a record must have, so that logs from different vendors can be read the same way.

subtitle: Recording what clients ask the routing system to do

tldr.problem: Software that programs routers can make many changes at once, so when something goes wrong there is no standard way to find out which client made which change and when.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a set of trace log fields that must appear in every I2RS trace log, covering the client, the operation requested and applied, the result code and the timings.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational framework: it fixes the fields and the ways to get the log out, but leaves storage, rotation and retention policy to whoever runs the system.

today: RFC 7922 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the traceability framework for the Interface to the Routing System work. It fixes the fields that must appear in a trace log and names one retrieval method as mandatory to implement, but leaves storage, rotation, retention and protection to the organisations running the system.

sections.title: Why Traceability Is Needed
sections.content:
The architecture for the Interface to the Routing System in RFC 7921 specifies that I2RS clients wishing to retrieve or change the routing state on a routing element must authenticate to an I2RS agent. The client has a unique identity it provides for authentication, and should provide another opaque identity for applications communicating through it. Programming routing state produces a return code containing the result of the specified operation and the associated reasons. All of this is critical information for understanding the history of I2RS interactions, and this document defines the framework necessary to trace those interactions, along with use cases, an information model and reporting requirements. Effective troubleshooting here means being able to identify what operation was performed by a specific I2RS client via the I2RS agent, what the result was, and when it was performed.

As networks scale and policy becomes an increasingly important part of the control plane that creates and maintains forwarding state, operational complexity increases as well. I2RS offers more granular and coherent control over policy and control-plane state, but it also removes or reduces the locality of the policy applied to the control plane at any individual forwarding device. The ability to automate and abstract even complex policy-based controls highlights the need for an equally scalable traceability function that records, at event-level granularity, the evolution of the routing system.
sections.plainLanguage: When policy moves out of the router and into software, the router itself no longer shows which rules were applied. A log of every change, with its origin and time, is the way to keep that knowledge.

sections.title: What the Log Is For
sections.content:
An obvious motivation is the need to troubleshoot and identify root causes of problems in increasingly complex routing systems. Since I2RS is a high-throughput multi-channel, full duplex and highly responsive interface, I2RS clients may be performing a large number of operations on I2RS agents concurrently, or at nearly the same time and quite possibly in very rapid succession. As these many changes are made, the network reacts accordingly, and those changes might lead to a race condition, performance issues, data loss or disruption of services. To isolate the root cause it is critical that an operator has visibility into what changes were made via I2RS at a specific time.

Some network environments have strong auditing requirements for configuration and runtime changes, and others have policies that require saving logging information for operational or regulatory compliance. These requirements demand that I2RS provides an account of changes made to network element routing systems.

As I2RS becomes more pervasive, a traceability model that supports controllable trace log retention using a standardised structured data format offers significant advantages, such as the ability to create common tools supporting automated testing. The document lists the use cases this enables: real-time monitoring and troubleshooting of router events; automated event correlation, trend analysis and anomaly detection; offline analysis, manual or tool-based, of router state evolution from the retained trace logs; enhanced network audit, management and forensic analysis capabilities; improved accounting of routing system operations; and a standardised format for incident reporting and test logging.
sections.plainLanguage: The log serves several jobs: finding out what went wrong, meeting audit rules, spotting patterns and anomalies over time, counting how much the routing system is being used, and giving everyone the same format to report incidents in.

sections.title: The Trace Log Fields
sections.content:
The fields listed in Section 5.2 comprise an I2RS trace log, and together they ensure that each interaction can be traced back to the client that made the request at a specific point in time. This list is a common set of fields that must appear in all I2RS trace logs; implementations may choose to log additional fields such as the I2RS client vendor or agent statistics like free memory and performance metrics.

Event ID is a unique identifier for each event in the log. An event can be a client authenticating with the agent, a client-to-agent operation, or a client disconnecting. Operation events can be logged atomically upon completion, in which case they carry both a Starting and an Ending Timestamp, or they can be logged at the beginning of each Request State transition. Because operations can occur from the same client at the same time, an identifier that can be unambiguously associated with a specific entry matters, and if each state transition is logged for an operation, the same ID must be used for each of those entries, so the life of a request can be followed in the log. Starting Timestamp is the time at which the operation enters the specified Request State within the agent; if the entry covers the whole request it is the time the request was first received. It must be present in entries that specify the beginning of a state transition and in those covering the whole request. The time uses the full timestamp format of RFC 3339, including the date and offset from Coordinated Universal Time, and because many operations can occur in rapid succession the fractional seconds element must be used to provide adequate granularity, expressed with at least three significant digits in second.microsecond format.

Request State is the state of the operation within the I2RS agent state machine at the given timestamps. The agent should generate a log entry at the moment a request enters and exits a state: on entry the entry has a Starting Timestamp and no Ending Timestamp, on exit an Ending Timestamp and no Starting Timestamp. The states are PENDING, where the request has been received and queued for processing; IN PROCESS, where it is currently being handled by the agent; and COMPLETED, where it has reached a terminal point. Every state transition should be logged unless that would put an undue performance burden on the agent, but an entry with the state COMPLETED must be logged for all operations, and if COMPLETED is the only entry for a request it must have both timestamps covering the entire duration from ingress to completion.

Client Identity is the identity the client used to authenticate to the agent. Client Priority is the priority assigned by the access control model that authenticates the client, for example by the NETCONF Access Control Model in RFC 6536. Secondary Identity is an opaque identity known to the client from a controlling network application, used to trace the application driving the client's actions; it must be logged even if the client does not provide one, in which case the field is empty. Client Address is the network address of the client that connected to the agent, which may be an IPv4 or an IPv6 address.

Requested Operation is the I2RS operation that was requested, for example an add route operation if a route is being inserted into a routing table, and it may not be the operation actually applied. For a client authenticating it must be CLIENT AUTHENTICATE, and for a client disconnecting it must be CLIENT DISCONNECT. Applied Operation is the operation that was actually performed, which can differ when the agent cannot satisfy the request; it may not be logged unless the Request State is COMPLETED. Operation Data Present is a Boolean field saying whether additional per-operation data is present. Requested Operation Data is the data passed to the agent, for a route add operation the route prefix, prefix length and next-hop information to be inserted, and the specific routing table the route will be added to. If operation data is provided, the Operation Data Present field must be TRUE; where an operation provides no data the field must be FALSE and the data field empty. When a client authenticates, the Requested Operation Data must contain the client priority, and other attributes such as credentials used for authentication may be logged. Applied Operation Data is the data actually applied, and can differ from the requested data if the agent could not satisfy the request with it; it stays empty unless requested data was specified, and may not be logged unless the Request State is COMPLETED.

Transaction ID shows that the operation is part of a long-running I2RS transaction made of multiple related operations, so several log entries can be related to one overall operation; it is optional and may not be logged unless the event is part of such a transaction. Result Code holds the result of the operation once the state is COMPLETED, and for Routing Information Base operations it must be the return code specified in the RIB Info Model; an operation may not complete with a result code in the case of a timeout, but a failed operation must still be logged with an appropriate result code. Timeout Occurred is a Boolean field saying whether a timeout happened, in which case the Ending Timestamp must be the time the agent recorded for the timeout; it may not be logged unless the state is COMPLETED. Ending Timestamp is the time at which the operation exits the specified state, and follows the same rules as the Starting Timestamp. End Of Message is an indicator that should mark the end of each log entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry records who was talking, what they asked for, what was really done, the answer, and when. Some entries are written when a request enters or leaves a processing step, and each such entry repeats the same event identifier so the whole life of the request can be read back.

sections.title: An Example Log Entry
sections.content:
Section 6 shows a sample of what the fields and values could look like. The entry records event ID 1, a starting timestamp of 2013-09-03T12:00:01.21+00:00, a request state of COMPLETED, a client ID of 5CEF1870-0326-11E2-A21F-0800200C9A66, a client priority of 100, a secondary ID of com.example.RoutingApp, a client address of 2001:db8:c0c0::2, a requested operation of ROUTE_ADD and an applied operation of ROUTE_ADD, operation data present as TRUE, requested and applied operation data of PREFIX 2001:db8:feed:: PREFIX-LEN 64 NEXT-HOP 2001:db8:cafe::1, a transaction ID of 2763461, a result code of SUCCESS(0), timeout occurred as FALSE, and an ending timestamp of 2013-09-03T12:00:01.23+00:00.

The example also shows why the end-of-message marker matters. Because the fields vary, implementors must use a format-appropriate indicator so that the end of one record can be told from the beginning of another: a newline character in a linear-formatted log similar to syslog, element tags denoting the beginning and end of records in an XML-formatted log, or record separation such as comma-separated array elements in a JSON-formatted log.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example is a route addition that succeeded: which client asked, what prefix and next hop it wanted, and when it started and finished. Because the fields differ in length, each record also needs a marker saying where it ends.

sections.title: Storing and Getting the Log Out
sections.content:
Specific operational procedures for temporary log storage, rollover, retrieval and access are out of scope, and organisations using I2RS trace logging are responsible for establishing procedures suited to their own requirements and environment. Section 7 gives only fundamental, implementation-independent guidance.

Creation. The I2RS agent interacts with the routing and signalling functions of the routing element. Because the agent is responsible for actually making the routing changes on the network device, it creates and maintains a log of operations that can be retrieved to troubleshoot I2RS-related impact on the network. Changes to the network element's local configuration made outside the I2RS protocol that preempt I2RS state are logged only if the network element notifies the agent.

Temporary storage. The trace information may be stored either in an in-memory buffer or as a file local to the agent. Care should be given to the number of I2RS operations expected on a given agent so the right storage medium is used, maximising the effectiveness of the log without harming the performance and health of the agent. Client requests may not always be processed synchronously or within a bounded time, so buffering of trace log entries may be required to keep fields such as Operation and Result Code in the same record; this buffering may add resource load on the agent and the network element. Rotating the trace log preserves the operation history without exhausting resources, and it is acceptable to use an in-memory buffer for recent operations while rotating or archiving older ones to a local file. The implementation details of the physical storage file, such as size, throughput and data protection, are out of scope. On retention, attention should be paid to how long log data is kept when it contains security- or privacy-sensitive attributes, because the longer it is retained the higher the impact if it leaks, and legislation may impose additional minimum or maximum retention periods.

Rotation. To prevent exhaustion of resources on the agent or its network device, it is recommended that the agent implement trace log rotation. The details are left to the implementation, but rotation by time or by size should be possible, and if file rollover is supported, multiple archived log files should be supported to maximise the troubleshooting and accounting benefits of the log.

Retrieval. Implementors are free to provide their own proprietary interfaces and custom tools, which may include displaying the trace log as command-line output. A key intention of the information model is to establish a vendor-agnostic and consistent interface for collecting the data, so retrieval should also be vendor-agnostic. Exporting the information must not interfere with the agent's ability to process new incoming operations. Three retrieval routes are described. The syslog protocol is a standard way of sending event notifications from a host to a collector, but it defines no standard format for storing the messages, so the data in a syslog message would follow the information model and be readable by a person but not easily parsed by a machine; where syslog is used, existing logging infrastructure should be leveraged without extending the formats, and the fields should be modelled and encoded as Structured Data Elements. The information collection mechanism of the I2RS architecture, which obtains a snapshot of a large amount of data from the network element, should be used to make the trace log available either as a single snapshot or via a subscription stream. And I2RS publish and subscribe is the mandatory-to-implement route: I2RS agents must support publishing trace log information to the feed of changes defined for the I2RS layer, so subscribers receive a live stream of I2RS interactions in trace log format and can log them to a datastore, aggregate and summarise interactions from a single client, and so on.
sections.plainLanguage: The agent writes the log, keeps it in memory or on disk, rotates it so it cannot fill the router, and offers it in three ways: as syslog messages, as a snapshot of router data, or as a live stream. The live stream is the one every implementation has to offer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The I2RS trace log, like any log file, reveals the state of the entity producing it as well as the identifying information elements and detailed interactions of the system containing it. The information model does not itself introduce security issues, but it does define the set of attributes that make up an I2RS log file. Those attributes may contain sensitive information and should therefore adhere to the security, privacy and permission policies of the organisation using the log file.

How to protect the stored log file is out of scope, but adequate precautions and security best practices are expected, such as disk encryption, appropriately restrictive file and directory permissions, suitable hardening and physical security of the logging entities, mutual authentication, transport encryption, and channel confidentiality and integrity when transferring log files. In addition, the potentially sensitive information in a log file should be adequately anonymised or obfuscated by operators to ensure its privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: A log of who changed what and when is sensitive in itself. The document does not say how to protect it, but expects ordinary care: encrypted disks, tight file permissions, secure transport, and masking of anything that identifies a person or a customer.

messages.note: Zero or more applications may drive client activity.

messages.note: One or more log entries record what was done, by which client, and when.

viz.caption: The three request states an operation can be logged in

items.title: PENDING
items.text: The request has been received and queued for processing.

items.title: IN PROCESS
items.text: The request is currently being handled by the I2RS agent.

items.title: COMPLETED
items.text: The request has reached a terminal point. An entry with this state must be logged for all operations.

viz.caption: The three ways of retrieving the trace log

cells: Standard event notifications to a collector. The protocol defines no storage format, so the fields should be encoded as Structured Data Elements.
The snapshot mechanism of the I2RS architecture, delivering the log as one snapshot or as a subscription stream.
Agents publish the log to the feed of changes, so subscribers receive a live stream of interactions in trace log format.
